extracted.intended_audience: researchers and authors reporting observational epidemiologic studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) for peer-reviewed publication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to report design-specific methods and results of observational epidemiology studies (cohort, case-control, cross‑sectional), including what data to present, how to present analyses, and how to interpret and discuss findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14(b) Report numbers with missing data for each variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate the number of participants with missing data for each variable of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should report amounts of missing data for exposures, potential confounders, and other important patient characteristics; in cohort studies also report extent of loss to follow-up with reasons. Missing data can bias results or affect generalisability. Use tables and figures to enumerate amounts of missing data. (See also item 12c and Box 6.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 14(c) Cohort study: Summarise follow-up time
rubrics_metrics.description: For cohort studies, summarise follow-up time—e.g., average and total amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present mean or median follow-up (or both) so readers can calculate person-years (mean × number of participants). Consider reporting minimum/maximum or percentiles to show spread. Report total person‑years or proportion of potential data captured. Present such information separately for participants in different exposure categories when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15 Outcome data: Report numbers of outcome events or summary measures over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Report numbers of outcome events or summary measures appropriate to the study design (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cohort: give numbers of events for each outcome, consider event rate per person‑year, and if risk changes over time present numbers/rates in intervals or Kaplan–Meier tables/plots (prefer cumulative incidence plots). Case-control: report numbers in each exposure category or summary measures of exposure (frequencies/quantitative summaries). Cross-sectional: report prevalent outcome events or summary measures. Consider presenting measures of association in the same table as descriptive data. Tabulating continuous outcomes/exposures in categories may be helpful even if not analyzed that way.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16(a) Main results: Give unadjusted and adjusted estimates and their precision; state confounders and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide unadjusted estimates and, when applicable, confounder‑adjusted estimates with measures of precision (e.g., 95% confidence intervals). Make clear which confounders were adjusted for and why they were included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present unadjusted analyses together with main data (e.g., counts of exposed/unexposed) so readers can understand the data behind measures of association. For adjusted analyses report number of persons included (may differ because of missing covariate data). Give confidence intervals. Explain all potential confounders considered and criteria for including/excluding variables, guided by knowledge or explicit causal assumptions. If selection of confounders was based on change-in-estimate or stepwise procedures, describe the process and the significance level used; avoid selecting confounders solely on statistical significance. Caution readers that adjusted results are not necessarily free from random error, selection or information bias, or residual confounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16(b) Report category boundaries when continuous variables were categorised
rubrics_metrics.description: When continuous variables are categorised, report the category boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorisation affects analysis and presentation. In tables, give outcomes for each exposure category (counts, person‑time if relevant) and, at minimum, report the category boundaries. It is helpful also to report range of the data and mean or median within categories. Note that quantile-derived categories' boundaries cannot be inferred from summary data, so explicitly report them to aid comparison and meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16(c) Translate relative effects into absolute risks when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: If relevant, consider translating estimates of relative risk into absolute risk for a meaningful time period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative measures (ratios) capture association strength and are commonly used, but absolute risks (e.g., additional cases per 1000 users over X years) are often of greater interest for impact and policy. Provide absolute measures (attributable risk, population attributable fraction) with measures of statistical uncertainty (confidence intervals) and report methods/formulae used to calculate them. Be aware of strong assumptions required (including causality) and discuss them. Present absolute and relative measures together when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box 7: Use appropriate measures of association and be explicit about concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly define and use appropriate measures (prevalence, incidence, cumulative incidence, incidence rate, relative risk, rate ratio, odds ratio, prevalence ratio) and consider whether relative or absolute measures better address the study question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational studies may describe magnitude/distribution (prevalence/incidence) or compare risks between exposed and unexposed (relative measures). Expressing results both in relative and absolute terms is often helpful. Understand the sampling implications for odds ratios in case-control studies and whether odds ratios estimate risk or rate ratios. For measures of impact (e.g., attributable fraction), be explicit about concepts and methods and avoid incorrect approaches to adjust for other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: 17 Other analyses: Report subgroup, interaction, and sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Report other analyses done such as subgroup analyses, interaction assessments, attributable risks, alternative variable definitions, and sensitivity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish analyses that were planned from those that were exploratory/unplanned, so readers can judge multiplicity. There is value in pre‑specified subgroup analyses (when adequately powered) but caution about post-hoc subgroup claims. Report whether and how interactions were assessed (additive vs multiplicative scales) and consider presenting separate and joint effects (e.g., in tables) with confidence intervals. Avoid inferring effect modification by comparing P-values across subgroups; directly test whether effect sizes differ. Use sensitivity analyses to assess robustness to analytic choices, missing data, or biases; report level of detail proportional to their importance—briefly state consistency if many were done, but provide details when an issue is of major concern or estimates vary substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box 8: Interaction (effect modification) — report and evaluate additive and multiplicative interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating joint effects of two exposures, assess interaction on additive and/or multiplicative scales and present separate and joint effects to allow readers to evaluate different interaction concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that relative risks imply multiplicative models while risk differences correspond to additive models; neither uniquely indicates biological mechanism. Present separate and joint effects (HuGENet layout recommended). When models estimate relative risks, these can be translated to an additive scale; present measures like the Relative Excess Risk due to Interaction (RERI) with confidence intervals. Avoid relying on inappropriate comparisons (e.g., overlapping CIs across subgroups) and report formal tests of interaction when claiming effect modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion structure: organise discussion to address validity and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the discussion to reduce over-interpretation and guide readers through validity and implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recommended structure: (1) brief synopsis of key findings; (2) consideration of possible mechanisms/explanations; (3) comparison with relevant published studies; (4) limitations of the study; and (5) brief summary of implications for practice and research. Link research recommendations to identified limitations and suggest how future research could improve on the study rather than merely stating 'more research is needed'. Consider using subheadings for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18 Key results: Summarise key results with reference to objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the discussion with a short summary of the main findings in relation to the study objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concise summary helps readers assess whether subsequent interpretations and implications are supported by the findings. Summaries should explicitly reference the original hypotheses or objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: 19 Limitations: Discuss limitations including sources, direction and magnitude of bias or imprecision
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and discuss study limitations, taking into account sources of potential bias or imprecision, and discuss both the likely direction and magnitude of any potential bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss biases (selection, information, confounding), loss to follow-up, non-participation, and measurement imprecision (attenuation/regression dilution). Consider study size and measurement issues; explain relative importance of different biases and compare validity, generalisability and precision with other studies to place the contribution in context. Don't omit important limitations; be explicit about how limitations could affect conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20 Interpretation: Give a cautious overall interpretation considering multiple sources of uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a cautious overall interpretation that considers objectives, limitations, multiplicity of analyses, results from similar studies, and other relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for confounding, sensitivity analyses, multiplicity/subgroup analyses, and residual confounding due to unmeasured or imprecisely measured variables. Address the real range of uncertainty, which exceeds statistical uncertainty in confidence intervals because design and measurement issues add uncertainty. Use Bradford Hill criteria as a heuristic for causal reasoning but not mechanically; weigh strength, temporality, consistency, experimental support, specificity, dose–response, plausibility, etc., while acknowledging limitations of each criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 21 Generalisability: Discuss external validity/applicability of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the generalisability (external validity) of the study results to other populations or settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalisability is meaningful only with respect to clearly specified conditions. Describe how the study sample, settings, and exposures compare to the target populations of interest and explain limitations to applying estimates elsewhere (for example, differences in patient mix, treatments, or baseline risks). Provide information (e.g., range of participants, countries/settings) that supports judgments about applicability.
